<|endoftext|>In order to manufacture a more compact, lighter and lighter-weight electronic product, the circuit board for the product tends to become thinner, smaller in size and lighter-weight. Electronic chips are also produced increasingly at the same time. Similarly, heat-generating elements such as power integrated circuits, diodes and the like tend to be developed in a chip of smaller and smaller size for functional improvement and for electronic product miniaturization.
In today`s technology, power elements are usually mounted on a circuit board by flip-chip bonding. As shown in FIG. 1(a), an integrated circuit (IC) chip 10 carrying electronic components is bonded on a metal sheet 20 through conductive bumps 13 on pads 21. An underlie under metal sheet (UBM) 30 passes through an insulating sheet 20, in order to transfer the heat generated by electronic circuit 1. FIG. 1(b) illustrates the underlie under metal sheet 30 mounted between the circuit board 1 and a heat slug 2.
The structure of the aforementioned set-up requires that the circuit board 1 must provide a heat dissipating space 3 and accommodate heat-generating elements 4, but it limits the number of heat-generating elements 4 to those without a direct connection to the circuit board. Further, it requires a heat-sink unit 5 to be separately placed to be disposed under the circuit board 1, and therefore the structure increases ratio of thicknesses.
A heat block 10 as shown in FIG. 2 is proposed as an updated structural solution to solve the aforementioned problems. With reference being made to FIG. 2, the heat block 10 comprises a circuit board 20 with a dielectric layer 150, with a border heater 200 located at the edge of dielectric layer 150, before a heat-generating electronic element 400 is inserted into circuit board 20. For transferring the heat generated by heat-generating electronic element 400, border heater 200 can be used only when electronic element 400 is assembled against circuit board 20.
On the other hand, a material which can improved heat conductivity is needed. <|endoftext|>Data protection problems and risks of network computing {#Sec1}
================================================================

Public concerns about risks from big data and the software crisis have led to the idea of an \"open office\" for network computing (CDA [@CR2]). According to this vision, information technology produces an out-of-control flood of data and a constant demand for more storage capacity and more computing power. This massive influx of data is accompanied by diminishing returns, rating risks as only moderate, because there is no danger from software errors and a benefit from reducing the time needed to find information and from conveniently storing large collections of information.

Challenges to this traditional vision have emerged, among them data protection (DPA) and data regulation. The question arises, how can current data protection problems be solved; will the creation of a wider range of data-processing devices exposing their critical security issues play out as it does in the pharmaceutical sector and in atomic energy? With the development of these devices, health care organizations and their competitors but also entrepreneurs and other \"start-ups\" have the strong

interest to use the security and confidentiality resources of \"big data\". This creates serious data protection risks. In the case of nuclear energy, the security problem dates back to military-civilian co-operation in Nazi Germany from 1939 to 1945. In the nuclear realm, the secrets of national security belonged to civilian organisations, military organisations and to the state as a joint work in which personal and national security had to go along with financial and infrastructural responsibilities and on the obligation to make cooperation with other government and technical authorities possible and possible. This historical background has given rise to significant data protection standards that can be found in all major guidelines for data protection. Some national and international organisations, regulations and standards (e.g. *Federal Data Protection Act*, Germany) have defined certain trust components for data (e.g. *Third party Principle*) and security (e.g. *Principle of Level 1* that concerns categorization of levels of risk) and defined detailed requirements. Implementation of these requirements is expected to become relatively easy and efficient in the near future. However, the current state of protection of data from loss, illegal or illegal traces has proven much harder. For example, a high burden of regulation (e.g. in economic networks *European Telecommunications Networks Initiative*, *EC Directive*) is the reason for a lessening or absence of knowledge of the real benefits of any savings in an \"open office\". <|endoftext|>Video communication using a packet network such as IP (Internet Protocol) Network can be carried out using, for example, a Mosaic-based server architecture for real-time video. If there is no delay between video frames to be communicated in real-time video communication, it is possible to provide high video quality by statistical coding of the video. If it is necessary to provide high-quality images even with means of low-delay communication in reflection communication along with voice communication, coding technologies (as described, for example, in p. 232 of vol. 15 of ITU-T, Recommendation H.263, “Video coding forporal-spatial addressing”*) that allow compression of a whole picture by two processes of inter-picture prediction and intra-picture coding without destroying the temporal and spatial correlation between pictures can be applied.
If the camera moves, the position of the picture to be communicated can change. In video communication using Mosaic-based server architecture, coding schemes that protect picture quality when the position of a picture to be communicated changes are available.
